events.reader:
Selected audience: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs.
Situation context (grounded; check applicability): This is an ops/IT-adjacent person at a company where policies and handbooks are written up in Notion or similar docs and employees communicate primarily in Slack; when someone can't find an answer, they ping this person (or the team channel) directly, and this person has been asked to build or is considering building an automated Slack responder that draws on the Handbook, Docs, and Issue Trackers.
events.reader_segment: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs
events.promise: The internal Slack answer-bot over your handbook is now something you configure and inspect, not something you assemble and then own.
events.arc: Single email, single movement: name what is now available in the terms of the thing this reader was already planning to build, show the two structural differences that matter to someone who has read the build guides (no vector store to run; every Slack answer lands as an inspectable run), and ask for one narrow test — one document set, one channel — rather than a decision.

emails.job: Get an ops/IT generalist who is planning or part-way into a homegrown Slack answer-bot to create one agent over one set of policy documents and ask it real questions in Slack this week.
emails.single_idea: The internal Slack answer-bot you were going to assemble is now something you configure: orqAgent installs into Slack by OAuth, answers from your own handbook documents with no vector store to stand up, and records what it did on every answer — which is the part a hand-wired workflow never gives you.
emails.objection: Nobody here owns internal tooling — who keeps this running after I build it?
must_not_say: No guardrail, PII-masking, content-filtering or prompt-injection claims — that capability state is unknown for this campaign, and this audience's research names no safety concern. The analytics fact may be used for latency, token usage and spend only; do not repeat its guardrail-rate clause.

No compliance or certification claims of any kind — not SOC 2 (it is only in progress), not HIPAA, not "compliant" in any form. Do not raise the security axis at all: the field is ahead of us there and the email loses on it.

No plan limits and no figures from the pricing tables — not credits, not executions, not runs per month, not the $29 price. The company's own pages contradict each other on Pro, and a number here invites the reader to go find the contradiction. The free plan may be named as the way in; the numbers may not.
No uptime or SLA language. The 99.9% figure is contractually guaranteed only on Enterprise, and uptime is a contested axis every competitor claims.
No customer names, logos, quotes, adoption counts or "teams like yours" — none exist in the material, and an invented one is the fastest way to lose a reader who will check.

No accuracy, deflection-rate, time-saved or ticket-reduction promise. Nothing in the evidence measures answer quality. Describe what the agent does and what the run record shows; invite the test, do not predict the result.

Do not describe retrieval as semantic, embedding-based, or as understanding paraphrased questions. What is licensed is: documents are uploaded, relevant context is retrieved automatically for every query, and there is no vector DB to manage. Nothing more.

Do not position this against a workspace AI assistant or a knowledge base the reader already pays for, by name or by implication. There is no answer in the evidence to "why add a third thing", and raising it hands the reader their own objection. The ask is to run one agent beside what exists.

Do not name or characterise competing tools' quality, breadth, speed or reliability. The reader's own low-code stack may be described only in the terms its own practitioners use — fast to build, not built for production observability.
Do not claim the agent replaces a backend, a helpdesk, a search tool or an operational workflow; and no SSO/SAML, no voice or telephony, no deep domain-specific integrations.

The rest of the integration list — WhatsApp, Telegram, Email Inbox, webhooks, Stripe — stays out. This email is Slack and documents. Every extra channel named is a reason for this reader to think it is not built for them.

Do not assert what this specific company's setup, tooling or past attempts are. Anything about a half-built bot or an abandoned project is conditional at best: "if you have already started wiring this up", never "you have".
Do not promise voice or telephony support unless a current licensed source explicitly establishes it.
Do not claim that the agent layer replaces a company's complete backend, product UI, billing, or operational workflow without direct evidence.
Compliance and certification claims are unavailable unless the Evidence Ledger explicitly licenses them.
Do not claim Knowledge base / RAG context; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Agent guardrails; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Reusable per-client agent configuration; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Voice and telephony runtime; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim Full SaaS backend replacement; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Deep domain-specific operational integrations; its capability state is unknown.

Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks (E56, E57) rather than semantic search, and the free tier caps the knowledge base at five documents (E120), so a question worded unlike the handbook or spread across a large page.

The 99.9% uptime figure is only contractually guaranteed on Enterprise (E147, E37), Starter keeps just 7 days of run history and Pro 30 days of analytics (E28, E32), and hitting the monthly quota returns a hard 429 (E129).
emails.felt_need: The same policy and handbook questions get asked repeatedly in Slack, and the answers are buried in documentation that is difficult to navigate.
emails.status_quo: Team members search Notion by trying random keywords or guessing document titles rather than getting a direct answer.
emails.why_it_fails: By the account of the practitioners who build it, that low-code stack is a jetpack, not a long-haul aircraft: it is not suited to high-scale, latency-sensitive or highly reliable production use, and it gives no deep observability. It also leaves the builder running a vector store purely so a bot can answer from a PDF, and nobody at the company owns internal tooling once the build is finished.
emails.mechanism: Three design decisions, all documented. Slack is a native OAuth install, so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages without a webhook service to keep alive. Documents are uploaded and the agent retrieves the relevant context for every query automatically — there is no vector database to manage. And observability is not something you configure: P95 latency, token usage per model and daily spend trends are tracked automatically, so the answer to "what did it do and what did it cost" exists on day one rather than being the dashboard nobody got around to building.

events.body:
The policy question lands in Slack mid-morning, and it lands with you.

The answer is in the handbook. Finding it takes several searches across pages whose titles nobody remembers — which is usually why the question came to a person instead.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and it is open to sign-ups now. The answer-bot over your handbook is a configuration on it rather than a build.

Slack connects by OAuth install, and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages. You upload PDFs, docs or plain text, and the agent retrieves the relevant context for every query — no vector DB to manage.

Which leaves the question of who keeps it running once the build is done. Setup happens in the console in under two minutes, and P95 latency, token usage per model and daily spend trends are tracked automatically, without extra config.

What it did, and what it cost, is on the record from the first answer.

> **One agent, one set of policy documents, one Slack channel** — then ask it the five questions your team asks most.
events.postscript: Starting is free and takes no card.

orqAgent is available today — a hosted place to configure one agent over your own handbook documents. Slack is an OAuth install, so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

You upload the PDFs, docs or plain text. The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage.

P95 latency, token usage per model and daily spend trends are tracked automatically, without extra config. What it answered and what it cost is a page you open, not a dashboard someone has to build.

> **Start for free** — one agent, one set of policy documents, one Slack channel, and the questions your team asks most.

events.brief_drift: The brief's assigned idea — the handbook stays where your team maintains it (Notion/Google Docs connected as sources) — is nowhere on the page; the email argues the nearby, upload-only idea instead, which the supplied ledger does justify (E11 is licensed, E94/E95/E60 are not), but nothing in the copy tells this reader whether the sources they were actually asked to cover are in scope.
events.critique_summary: Stop asserting a build this reader hasn't made and actually answer the ownership question the opener raises, cut the unattributed low-code reliability verdict where every reader stopped, and make clear that one agent sits over a set of documents searched together — not one PDF.

edits.line: The question is not whether you can build a Slack answer-bot over the handbook. It is who owns it in March, when whoever built it has moved on.
edits.problem: It asserts a history this reader is not established to have — a build already done and a builder already departed — and then never answers the ownership question it opens; the body moves to features and the closing asks for a free trial, so the objection the email was assigned to kill is raised and left hanging. All three readers named this line, and two stopped reading at or immediately after it.
edits.fix: Make the ownership stake conditional on the build they may or may not have started ("if you wire this up yourself…"), and close the loop later in the body with the supported answer the email already owns: this is hosted and configured, so the thing they would otherwise inherit and maintain is not theirs to keep running. No new capability required — just the promise the subject line already makes, stated once in the body.

edits.line: A low-code stack gets a bot answering fast. By the account of the people who build them, it is not made for reliable production use — and it leaves you running a vector store so a bot can answer from a PDF.
edits.problem: This is where all three readers stopped. The reliability verdict is second-hand and unattributed ("the people who build them"), it reads as a knock rather than a fact, and it opens a reliability axis this email is explicitly barred from answering for itself — so the reader is handed a doubt about production reliability with nothing to settle it. It is also the third consecutive paragraph before orqAgent is named or described.
edits.fix: Keep only the concrete, checkable half — the vector store they would be running and the tooling nobody at the company owns afterwards — and drop or properly ground the production-reliability verdict. Compressing this beat also gets "orqAgent is available today" up a paragraph, which is where attention is currently being lost.

edits.line: Start for free — one agent, one set of policy documents, one Slack channel, and the questions your team asks most.
edits.problem: The triple "one… one… one" reads as a toy to a reader who was asked to cover Handbook, Docs and Issue Trackers: two readers said explicitly that one agent over one set of documents is not something they can evaluate against their actual ask. Nothing on the page says an agent can sit over several documents at once, even though E11 licenses exactly that ("upload PDFs, docs or plain text… retrieves the most relevant context for every query").
edits.fix: Scope the first test honestly without shrinking it: make plain that the documents you put behind one agent are plural and searched together for every question. Do not invent connectors, issue-tracker sync or source coverage the ledger does not license — narrow the ask to what upload supports and let the plural do the work.

edits.line: Subject: A Slack handbook bot you configure, not maintain  /  orqAgent: configure the handbook bot, don't build it
edits.problem: The subject and the headline make the same point in the same words, so the headline — the first thing read after the open — buys nothing. The brief also asked the subject to carry the one word that separates this from the build guides: that the answers are recorded. Neither line carries it.
edits.fix: Let one of the two carry configuration and the other carry the recorded run — the answers and what they cost are logged — so the headline advances the subject instead of repeating it.

edits.line: P.S. Setup runs from the console in under two minutes, and no credit card is required to start.
edits.problem: E130 licenses "create your first agent in under 2 minutes, no credit card required" — the subject is creating the agent, not setup end to end, which here also includes the Slack OAuth install and uploading documents. The line quietly widens the two minutes to cover the whole install.
edits.fix: Restate the timing against the documented subject (creating the first agent), leaving the card-free start as is.

events.body:
orqAgent is **available today** — a hosted place to configure one agent over your own policy documents and put it into Slack.

The same handbook questions keep coming back, and the answers sit in documentation that takes several searches to turn up.

Upload the PDFs, docs or plain text you already keep. The agent searches across all of them and retrieves the most relevant context for every question — **no vector DB to manage**.

Slack is an OAuth install, so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages. No event handler to stand up, no infrastructure to manage.

If you wire this up yourself, the part that outlasts the build is who keeps it running. Configured here, there is nothing left over to inherit — the platform is hosted, and setup happens in a console.

Analytics take no extra configuration: P95 latency, token usage per model and daily spend trends are tracked automatically. What the agent answered, and what it cost, is a page you open.

Start for free — put the policy documents your team asks about behind one agent, connect one Slack channel, and ask the five questions that come back every week.
